model.title: Falcon 9 / Starlink training mission
model.intro: This is a numerical demonstration with a reduced payload and return to the ground. Readings are computed from a single flight state. They are not telemetry from a real SpaceX launch.
model.formulas:
q = ½ρv² DYNAMIC PRESSURE
D = CdqA DRAG FORCE
a = (T + D) / m − μr / |r|³ VECTOR EQUATION OF MOTION
model.included.title: What is included
model.included.text: A spherical rotating Earth, gravity, changing atmospheric density, Mach-dependent drag, thrust and fuel consumption. Air speed includes the atmosphere co-rotating with the Earth. The orbit is determined from position and inertial velocity, not from altitude alone.
model.limits.title: Model limits
model.limits.text: Translational motion is computed in 3D. Attitude follows an approximate guidance program; rotational dynamics, wind, real control-surface aerodynamics and CFD are not modeled. Engine performance, masses and C<sub>d</sub> are public data and labeled engineering approximations. The return allows deep throttling; the landing burn is longer than in a typical real mission. Exhaust volume effects are visual shaders, not gas-dynamics computation.
model.limits.orbit: The separation orbit differs from the working orbit of the constellation. Raising the orbit with the satellites' electric thrusters and the months of operation that follow are not part of this demonstration.
model.plume.title: Plume expansion and the Kármán line
model.plume.text:
As ambient pressure drops, gases behind the nozzle expand more strongly: the narrow jet gradually turns into a wide, rarefied plume. Plume size and color in the shader are a visual approximation driven by the calculated ambient pressure, not CFD. The transition is smooth and starts well below 100 km. The Kármán line at 100 km is a conventional edge of space; the atmosphere still exists at that altitude.

model.disposal.title: Upper-stage disposal
model.disposal.text: After deployment, a calculated retrograde burn lowers perigee to −60 km. Heating is visualized below 120 km on descent; illustrative breakup occurs at 70 km. Remnants use one reference trajectory with approximate drag. Glow, fragment count, destruction and splashes are artistic interpretations, not CFD, thermal analysis or predictions of real debris. The long coast is accelerated; the finale takes 20 seconds of playback.
